figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: State-of-the-art CC-ReID experts make different mistakes: We consider here DIFFER and SapiensID on CHIRLA [22], a challenging multi-camera scenario. Left: two queries on which the experts disagree, with their top-3 candidates; green marks correct identities, red incorrect ones. Each model succeeds where the other fails. Middle: an oracle selecting the better model per query gains 13.5 rank-1 points over the best expert (dashed). Right: queries split by top-1 agreement and by which model is correct. Agreement is a reliable correctness signal, and in the disagreement column only 13% of queries have no correct candidate in either top-6 list. In this paper, we introduce and evaluate different approaches to rerank the union of both shortlists with a VLM judge, on every query or, to save compute, only where the two disagree.
figures.headline: An oracle that picks the better expert per query gains 13.5 rank-1 points, and top-1 agreement signals correctness.
citing_sentences: In Fig. 1 we show that for this pair, an oracle selecting the better expert per query exceeds the stronger of the two by 13.5 rank-1 (R-1) points on the multi-camera scenario of CHIRLA [22], a CC-ReID benchmark recorded over seven months.
Reranking every query with a VLM is expensive, and on queries the models already resolve it rarely changes the outcome while risking the demotion of a correct rank 1, as previously shown in Fig. 1.
Table 1 extends the oracle and error analysis of Fig. 1 to all four scenarios.

abstract: Cloth-changing person re-identification (CC-ReID) is still very challenging, and no method clearly dominates: methods that lead on one benchmark collapse on the others, because they rest on different identity cues. We show that a general-purpose vision-language model (VLM), used zero-shot as a judge for reranking a short candidate list, beats the expert retrieval models it reranks by a wide and consistent margin. On the four scenarios of CHIRLA, a long-term CC-ReID benchmark that no publicly released Re-ID model is trained on, reranking the candidates of two frozen experts raises rank-1 on every scenario, by $12.9$ points on average over the best expert and $9.4$ over the best naive ensemble of the two, with no component fine-tuned on the target data. Merging both experts’ shortlists matches or beats reranking the stronger expert’s shortlist alone, at lower cost. Introducing a VLM does, however, come at a cost: almost all of the pipeline’s FLOPs are spent on it. We therefore borrow a criterion from ensembling and invoke the VLM judge only where the two experts disagree at rank 1. This threshold-free gate removes $40\%$ of the calls, and a comparable share of total compute, with no significant drop in rank-1, trading $1.8$ to $3.8$ points of mAP. Judging remains the dominant cost, but on a benchmark where dedicated experts stall, we find a frozen general-purpose model to be the strongest judge of identity. The code is available at https://github.com/bdager/JudgeReID.

sections.body: The paper addresses cloth-changing person re-identification, where no single expert wins on every benchmark. The two frozen experts, DIFFER and SapiensID, make complementary errors. On the multi-camera scenario of CHIRLA, an oracle that picks the better expert per query gains 13.5 rank-1 (R-1) points over the stronger expert. When the two experts agree at rank 1, that shared prediction is correct for 85% of agreements on this scenario. The authors therefore propose a training-free ensemble in which a general-purpose vision-language model judges the union of both experts' top-k candidates. Gating the judge to queries where the experts disagree removes 40% of reranker calls, with no significant drop in R-1, at a cost of 1.8 to 3.8 mAP points.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Two CC-ReID experts make different errors, so a VLM judge over their merged shortlists could help.

sections.body: The related work covers three areas. Clothing-change methods remove clothing cues from identity features at training time. DIFFER disentangles identity from clothing over a frozen vision-language backbone, and SapiensID unifies face and body recognition. Vision-language models have been used for re-identification either as training-time signals or as standalone matchers, as in Duan et al., who evaluate six off-the-shelf models directly. Re-ranking and fusion methods such as RRF and score fusion treat both models symmetrically on every query. The authors place their method between these lines by invoking a vision-language model as an arbiter only where the experts disagree.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior work uses language in training or as a standalone matcher, not as an arbiter over expert shortlists.

sections.body: Two frozen experts retrieve independently from the gallery. If their rank-1 identities match, the default expert's ranking is returned unchanged. If they differ, the top-k matches of both experts form a candidate pool, which the vision-language model reorders in a single multi-image prompt. The head of the final ranking takes the first `k_H` reordered candidates. The tail comes from the expert that contributed most head candidates, with ties resolved toward the default expert. Duplicate images are resolved so that every gallery image appears exactly once. The prompt states each image's role and burns a label into each crop, because the authors report that position and recency effects bias multi-image answers. The pool ordering is treated as a design choice whose sensitivity is measured separately.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: Training-free arbitration: a VLM reranks the union of candidates only where the two experts' rank-1 identities disagree.

sections.body: CHIRLA is an evaluation-only long-term benchmark of seven months, with seven cameras and 22 identities. Metrics are rank-1 (R-1) and mean average precision (mAP), with significance from an exact sign-flip test over identities. The best gated configuration, with a pool of P=16, reaches 64.35 average R-1, which is 12.9 points above SapiensID, with a 95% confidence interval of [9.3,16.8]. Score fusion reaches 54.99, and the gain over it is significant in every scenario. The judge is the frozen Qwen3.6-27B model. A second model, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, scores 1.4 R-1 points lower on average and produces more invalid outputs. Qualitative examples show one correct recovery and one failure, where the judge misjudges gender from long hair.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: The gated VLM judge raises average rank-1 by 12.9 points over SapiensID on CHIRLA's four scenarios.

sections.body: The authors conclude that a general-purpose vision-language model judges identity better than either expert it reranks, with no training on the target data. Merging the two shortlists costs less than reranking a single expert's list at the same budget. Gating on rank-1 disagreement removes 40% of the calls with no significant loss in R-1, at a cost of 1.8 to 3.8 mAP. The stated limitations are that the evaluation uses only CHIRLA's 22 identities, so disagreement rates may differ elsewhere. The judge remains the dominant cost even when gated. It is also sensitive to candidate order and sometimes groups candidates by coarse attributes such as apparent gender.
sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.headline: Gating removes 40% of judge calls for a 1.8 to 3.8 mAP cost, and the results rest on CHIRLA's 22 identities.

sections.body: The appendix gives CHIRLA scenario sizes, with subset 0 excluded from reported metrics as the validation subset. It defines the FLOPs estimate as the forward cost of the experts plus `2N_act D` for the judge, omitting attention's context-dependent term and the vision encoder pass. It describes the three aggregation baselines, Borda voting, score fusion, and RRF with k=60. It reports results for pool sizes from 6 to 40. Uncertainty uses bootstrap replicates that resample identities. The median paired half-width is 1.5 points against 5.0 for single-method intervals. It also lists the prompt templates and a removal study of prompt components, none of which is significant.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists dataset statistics, FLOPs calculation, ensemble baselines, full pool-budget results, uncertainty estimates, prompt templates, and tail-rule ablation.
